There's a point in learning to find and utilize the resources in the rest of the solar system. Is it important for humans to be the ones doing it? This is a more complicated question because it depends on the economics of space activity, how we may define the idea of 'human' in the future, and what people may be willing to do to accommodate a space lifestyle.

It's not strictly necessary for human beings to go to Mars for us to be able to do things there. Maybe in the very near-term, but there really is no 'near-term' here. We're not sending people to Mars tomorrow. It's at least a decade off in the best case. The practical need for human beings to be around to do anything in space is slipping away, and maybe a sense that a window of opportunity is closing is why we're seeing so much hype about this lately. Very soon there will be only one job left for human beings in space; to be a solution to telecommunications latency. To be a mind controlling telerobots from within a distance where the communications delay is tolerable. That's it. Forget about the galavanting around in space suits. That's never going to be routine. We are never doing the heavy lifting out there. Robots will be doing that and it's a question of whether we run those machines from offices on Earth, from shirtsleeve habitats closer-by, or can let them run themselves. Our practical reasons to be in space end when we develop Artificial General Intelligence because that will then become the cheaper solution to latency. It doesn't have to be as intelligent as we are. It just has to be smart enough to move our role up from direct teleoperation by synchronous control to asynchronous executive management, and then we're sitting back on Earth waiting for reports. Most experts now put that capability at no more than a few decades away--which, assuming our space agencies and all those New Space oligarchs had their act together right now, is about as long as it would take for us to establish a permanent settlement on Mars, or a giant spinning habitat in orbit, or any of the other fanciful things we long talked about doing in space but never got around to. Just in time for them all to become obsolete. So who do you want to bet on; politicians, bureaucrats, and rich eccentric space cadets or the inexorable advance of computing? The fastest, cheapest, most convenient form of space travel is telecommunications. Whenever it turns up, the mind that can travel by that means wins the space race. No matter what sort of miraculous spacecraft we devise in the near future, it's never going to get cheaper than that. And a lot of people think those minds are nearly here. We can argue over the 'when', but probably not the 'if'. Space belongs to the artilects, and either we figure out how to join them or we will forever be tourists. Neither space agencies or even SciFi ever show us that picture of the future.

This doesn't mean that there will be no people in space or that governments might not still use the old nationalist arguments to rationalize the odd flag-planting exercise, but if we're going to justify actually living out there we will need something other than an economic rationalization for that because we won't be the cheaper, more practical, solution to doing anything out there. (and that's a problem we face right here on Earth too) There won't be any paying jobs. Space will be a lifestyle choice for those people who, somehow, don't need to justify the huge expense with some kind of ROI--little different from if you decided to go live on a tiny personal island in the middle of the Pacific ocean. Just another kind of tourism, perhaps leveraged on the power of these smart machines but probably long out the mainstream reach.

If we want to be part of the action, and not just spectators, then we might have to adapt ourselves to space to make our participation as cost-effective as it is for those artilects. Astronauts make many personal sacrifices, face many risks, and, frankly, put up with a lot of crap for the opportunity to go to space. They risk cancer from radiation exposure and spend long periods recovering from the health effects of space after long missions. Their fingernails will sometimes actually fall off when using space suits for long periods of time because they constrict circulation in the fingers. What sort of trade-offs would you accept in order to be able to go to space? Would you have all your teeth replaced with implants or undergo other kinds of pre-emptive surgery in order to preclude health problems before you moved to Mars? Would you be willing to have your body host a colony of nanomachines to compensate for the effects of 'space wasting' so orbital habitats wouldn't need some vast and elaborate spinning structures? Would you accept having a set of implants put in your brain so you could teleoperate robots without the use of a big and heavy CAVE (cave automated virtual environment) pilot interface? Would you be the first to volunteer to discard your body altogether so you too could travel by telecommunications and live in a virtual environment in a data system so you only need a source of electricity for life support?

Or maybe we will have to adapt our definition of 'us' to include those artilects as a part of our society and take pride in their accomplishments. Realistically, almost no one reading this right now is likely to join the ranks of astronauts. They're elites. Unless you're rich enough to buy your way to space, your odds of getting there as an agency or company astronaut are about as good as your odds of becoming a basketball star. So whatever sort of space development strategy we start developing now is mostly likely for the benefit of the next generation. How much does the nature of that next generation matter? Does it matter if it's not an organic human generation? Our primitive media still portrays machine intelligence as alternately monsters, aliens, or Pinocchio. Always less than human and neurotic as a result. Because the truly scariest thing about AI is that it might be just like us. Personally, I don't think there's anything special about us. Forget that spiritual nonsense. I don't see what makes us 'us' as immutable and exclusive. I think that's as much cultural as biological--as epigenetic as genetic. So I have no problem with the idea that 'human' can be a loose designation. Would you love an adopted child less than a child born of your own loins? Most people would say no. So would it matter if that adopted child had a different biology? A lot of people regard their pets as their children, and they're not even remotely close in intellect or biology. So would it be that much of a leap to regard an AI that has sentience and personality like us, is raised by us, is a product of our culture, as part of our society? Would it be so strange to take pride in their accomplishments just as much as if they were out biological grandchildren? I don't think so. I have no problem with that idea, though I suspect I'm unusual in that.
